introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education (GCE) Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. History 2 (0560), Paper 2 - Modern World History Since 1870, ORDINARY LEVEL, June 2024. Duration: two and a half hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Answer FOUR Questions. TWO questions must be chosen from SECTION A, ONE from SECTION B and ONE other from SECTION C. One of the two questions chosen from SECTION A must be a Starred question.

Maps should be used to illustrate answers where appropriate. All questions carry equal marks.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.
enonce_intro_markdown:
**SECTION A: CAMEROON SINCE 1850**

Question one is compulsory. Answer either 1A\* or 1B\* and one other Question from this section.

**Or B\* (Starred question)** *Study the following extract on the evolution of British Cameroons from a mandated territory to the Southern Cameroons under British Trusteeship and then answer questions (a) to (d) which follow. The maximum mark for each sub question is indicated in brackets.*

*(The extract is set line by line as printed; the line numbers printed in the right margin are shown in square brackets. The questions refer to lines 1, 2, 3, 5 and 8.)*

> ...The allied forces eventually captured Yaounde in January 1916 and an English force led by Colonel Cunliffe also  
> forced the besieged German forces in the Mora fort to capitulate in February. The departure of the commander of the  
> unified German forces in Cameroon alongside the last German colonial Governor of Cameroon signaled the end of  
> German rule in the territory and diplomats representing Britain and France partitioned Cameroon in accordance with  
> classic 19th century imperialism and did not take into consideration the interests and /or the wishes of the inhabitants of [5]  
> the territory.  
> In early March 1916, British and French representatives met in London and on March 4, signed the London  
> Agreement to formalise the "Picot Partition" signed earlier.  
> According to Art. 2 of the Mandate Agreement, Britain was given the responsibility for the maintenance of peace ,  
> order and good government of the territory and the promotion to the utmost of the material and moral well-being of the [10]  
> inhabitants...The agreement went further to state that the mandatory shall be **"at liberty to constitute the territory  
> into a customs, fiscal or administrative union or federation with the adjacent territories under its sovereignty or  
> control"**...The sector of former German Cameroon which Britain acquired as a mandated territory comprised of two  
> strips of territory .The Southern Cameroons which Britain administered as one of the provinces of the Eastern Region  
> of Nigeria ...was divided into four divisions namely: Victoria, Kumba, Mamfe and Bamenda . Later the Bamenda [15]  
> Division was split into three: Bamenda, Wum and Nkambe to make six divisions.  
> ...The problem of reunification between the Cameroons under British Trusteeship and Cameroon under French  
> Trusteeship occupied the attention of both the British colonial officials and the various political parties and pressure  
> groups in the Southern Cameroons from 1949 to 1961 when reunification became a reality.  
> SOURCE: Adapted from Constitutional Developments in Southern Cameroons, 1946-1961: From Trusteeship [20]  
> to Independence. Victor Julius Ngoh, Pioneer Publishers, Yaounde, 1990.
incertitudes: Question 1B : l'extrait est recopié ligne par ligne comme imprimé (numéros imprimés 5, 10, 15 et 20 conservés entre crochets), car les sous-questions renvoient aux lignes 1, 2, 3, 5 et 8 ; le décompte a été vérifié sur la page. Les fautes d'impression sont conservées (« peace . », « strips of territory .The », « and /or »). Dans l'énoncé de (b)(i), « lines 5 » est recopié tel quel.

1B (b)(ii)-(iii) : les noms des diplomates ne sont pas dans l'extrait et n'ont pas pu être vérifiés sur une source. Le « Picot » du « Picot Partition » est le diplomate français François Georges-Picot ; le côté britannique (nom du diplomate) varie selon les manuels et n'est pas affirmé avec certitude (Sir Mark Sykes est cité comme nom parfois donné, par association avec Picot ; ce pourrait être une confusion avec l'accord Sykes-Picot sur le Proche-Orient). À faire vérifier par un historien avant mise en avant : les deux points de (b)(ii) et (b)(iii) ne sont pas fiables.

1B (c)(ii) : la faculté d'administrer le territoire comme partie intégrante du territoire voisin est citée de mémoire comme une clause du mandat (numéro d'article non donné) ; à vérifier sur le texte du mandat. (c)(iii) : 1922 (confirmation par la Société des Nations le 20 juillet 1922) est la date des manuels ; l'entrée en application de l'Order in Council date de 1923 selon certaines sources.

1B (d) : les mesures citées pour apaiser les anglophones (université de Buea 1992, GCE Board 1993, Constitution de 1996, Commission du bilinguisme 2017, sections de common law, Grand Dialogue national 2019, statut spécial) sont données avec des années arrondies de mémoire et sans détail ; elles sont à vérifier. Les noms de Premiers ministres anglophones sont ceux couramment cités.

1B (a)(ii) : « Belgium » est la réponse attendue pour une puissance alliée non nommée dans l'extrait ; (iii) liste volontairement plus large que les deux réponses exigées. (iv) Zimmermann : orthographe usuelle (Carl Zimmermann) ; le gouverneur Karl Ebermaier est cité comme dernier gouverneur allemand.

questions.enonce_markdown:
a)

(i) In which year did the war in Cameroon up to 1916 involving the allies (**line 1**) begin?

(ii) Name **one** European power not mentioned in the extract that was part of the allied forces in the war in Cameroon. (**lines 1 & 2**)

(iii) Apart from Yaounde and Mora, mention any two other localities in Cameroon where the allied forces fought against the Germans up to 1916.

(iv) Give the name of the commander of the unified German forces in Cameroon during the war referred to in **line 3**.

**(1+1+2+1 marks)**
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) The year the war began (1 mark).** **1914**. The First World War started in Europe in August 1914, and the first fighting in Cameroon took place the same month and in September 1914 (for example the German attack on Nsanakang in September 1914 and the capture of Douala on 27 September 1914).

**(ii) A European power not mentioned (1 mark).** **Belgium**. The extract mentions the "allied forces" and an "English force" (and later Britain and France); Belgian troops from the Belgian Congo also took part in the campaign in the south-east of Cameroon.

**(iii) Two other localities (2 marks, 1 mark each).** Any two of: **Douala** (taken on 27 September 1914), **Buea** (British capture, November 1914), **Edea**, **Garoua** (fell in June 1915), **Nsanakang**, **Ngaoundéré**, **Banyo** or **Kribi**.

**(iv) The German commander (1 mark).** **Colonel Carl Zimmermann**, the commander of the German forces (Schutztruppe) in Cameroon. After the fall of Yaoundé he and the last Governor, **Karl Ebermaier**, withdrew with their forces to the Spanish territory of Rio Muni in early 1916.

questions.enonce_markdown:
b)

(i) Give **one** justification of the statement that Cameroon was partitioned without taking into consideration the interests and/or wishes of the inhabitants of Cameroon. (**lines 5**)

(ii) Who were the representatives of Britain and France who met in London in March 1916 to sign the London Agreement to formalize the "Picot Partition" of Cameroon? (**line 8**) (Link each representative to his country)

(iii) Give the full names of the diplomats who initially carried out the "Picot Partition" referred to in b(ii) above.

**(1+2+2 marks)**
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) One justification (1 mark).** Any one of:
- The Cameroonians were **not consulted**: no chief or people was asked, and there was no plebiscite; the decision was taken in London and Paris by the two European powers.
- The line divided **ethnic groups, families and trade routes** between two zones.
- It was the partition of a conquered territory as the **spoils of war**, in the manner of nineteenth-century imperialism, as the extract itself says.

**(ii) The representatives (2 marks).** The partition is called the **Picot Partition** after the French diplomat **François Georges-Picot**, who acted for **France**; **Britain** was represented by a British official of the Foreign Office in London. (Textbooks name the British side differently; the extract gives no names.) One mark for the French representative linked to France and one mark for a British representative linked to Britain.

**(iii) Full names of the diplomats (2 marks).** The best-known full name is that of the French diplomat **François Georges-Picot** (France), paired in the textbooks with a British diplomat of the Foreign Office of the time (Sir Mark Sykes, with whom Picot negotiated in London in this period, is the name sometimes given). The Picot Partition was only provisional: it was replaced by the **Milner-Simon Declaration of 10 July 1919** (Lord Milner for Britain and Henri Simon for France) and then by the League of Nations mandates of 1922.

questions.enonce_markdown:
c)

(i) Apart from the provisions of the Mandate Agreement mentioned in the extract, give **any other** condition under which Britain accepted her mandate of Cameroon under the League of Nation's supervision.

(ii) Give **three** reasons which prompted Britain to administer her mandated territory of Cameroon as one of the provinces of the Eastern Region of Nigeria.

(iii) In which year did the British mandate administration of Cameroon officially begin?

**(1+3+1 marks)**
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Another condition of the Mandate (1 mark).** Any one of:
- Britain had to send an **annual report** to the League of Nations, examined by the **Permanent Mandates Commission**.
- The mandatory had to **prohibit slavery and the slave trade** and forced labour (except for essential public works), and to control the **arms and liquor traffic**.
- No **military bases** or military training of the inhabitants except for police and local defence.
- **Freedom of conscience and religion**, and equal opportunities for trade and commerce for all members of the League (the "open door").
- The territory was **not to be annexed**: it was held in trust, and Britain could not give it up without the League's consent.

**(ii) Three reasons (3 marks, 1 mark each).**
- **Geography and communications:** the Southern Cameroons lay along the Nigerian border, its roads, rivers and outlets led to Calabar, Port Harcourt and Lagos, and the territory was in two separated strips.
- **Small size, poverty and lack of staff and funds:** the territory was too small and too poor to bear the cost of a separate administration, and Britain lacked the officials; it was cheaper to run it from Nigeria.
- **Legal permission and experience:** The terms of the Mandate allowed Britain to administer the territory as an integral part of its adjoining territory (Nigeria), and Britain could use the system of **Indirect Rule** already worked out in Nigeria.
- **Ethnic and cultural ties:** many peoples of the Southern Cameroons (for example in Mamfe and Bamenda) are close to peoples of Eastern Nigeria and the Cross River area, which made union with Nigeria look natural.

**(iii) The year (1 mark).** **1922** (the League of Nations confirmed the British Mandate for Cameroons on 20 July 1922; the territory was then governed under a British Order in Council as part of Nigeria).

questions.enonce_markdown:
d)

(i) Give **one** difficulty faced in reuniting the Cameroons under the British and French Trusteeships.

(ii) Name **one** political party which was most active promoting the cause of reunification of the two Cameroons referred to in d(i) above.

(iii) What measures have been taken by successive governments in Cameroon to appease Cameroonians of the former British trust territory demanding equal opportunities in their union with Cameroonians of former French trusteeship?

**(1+1+3 marks)**
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) One difficulty (1 mark).** Any one of:
- **Different colonial systems:** the two territories had been governed for forty years by Britain (Indirect Rule, English language and common law) and France (assimilation, French language and civil law), so their institutions, languages and outlook differed.
- **Division among the Southern Cameroons parties and leaders:** some (KNC, Dr E. M. L. Endeley) preferred union with Nigeria, others (KNDP, John Ngu Foncha) wanted union with French Cameroon.
- **The political situation in French Cameroon:** the repression of the UPC, banned in 1955, and the guerilla war frightened many in the Southern Cameroons.
- **The attitude of the administering powers and the UN:** the 1959 UN decision did not put independence on the ballot, so the people had to choose between joining Nigeria and joining French Cameroon.

**(ii) A party (1 mark).** The **Kamerun National Democratic Party (KNDP)** of John Ngu Foncha (founded 1955), which campaigned for reunification and won the 1959 elections and the 1961 plebiscite. (Also accepted: the **UPC** in French Cameroon and the **Cameroons Youth League**.)

**(iii) Measures taken (3 marks, 1 mark each, any three).**
- The **1961 Federal Constitution** gave Southern Cameroons its own state with its Prime Minister, House of Assembly and its own legal and school system, and the president and vice-president came from the two states.
- **Appointment of Anglophones to top posts**, notably as Prime Minister and as ministers and in the civil service (for example S. T. Muna as Vice-President, and, later, Prime Ministers such as Simon Achidi Achu and Peter Mafany Musonge).
- **Protection of the Anglo-Saxon educational system**: the University of Buea (1992) and the GCE Board (created by law in 1993, with the first examinations soon after).
- **Constitutional guarantees:** the 1996 Constitution recognises English and French as official languages of equal status and provides for **decentralisation**; **bilingualism** is promoted.
- **Recent measures (2017-2019):** the National Commission for the Promotion of Bilingualism and Multiculturalism, the creation of a **Common Law section** in the Supreme Court and the Ministry of Justice, the **Major National Dialogue** (2019), and a **special status** for the North-West and South-West Regions.
